newsitem.title: TURKEY: Jail riot deaths underline Turkey's Kurdish dissent.
newsitem.headline: Jail riot deaths underline Turkey's Kurdish dissent.

text.p: Turkey's efforts to end a festering Kurdish revolt has run into fresh trouble with a jail riot that killed eight people.
Eight Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) inmates died in a riot at Diyarbakir high-security jail on Tuesday before security forces brought the unrest under control.

"We know of eight dead," a hospital source told Reuters. He said 17 people were injured in the incident, sparked by a prisoner protest against the government's failure to improve prison conditions after a nationwide hunger strike in July.

Turkey has focused much of its attention for the last three weeks on trying to stem any knock-on effects that the upheaval in neighbouring Iraq's Kurdish region might have on Turkey's own restive Kurds.
Turkish security forces have launched big offensives against PKK rebels this week, highlighting the extent of separatist strife on Turkey's soil.
Around 20,000 troops backed by air power are involved in an anti-rebel push in the mountains of Tunceli province where the military says 15 guerrillas have been killed since Monday.
More than 20,000 people have been killed since 1984 in clashes between government forces and the rebels in a bitter fight that costs Turkey an estimated $8 billion annually.
Successive governments have refused to discuss demands by the rebels and non-violent Kurdish activists for self rule.
Ankara's effort to carve out a so-called security zone in northern Iraq, where Turkish Kurd rebels have bases, has also been sharply criticised by much of the Arab world.
The European Parliament last week threatened to block millions of dollars of European Union aid to Turkey because of its human rights record, sullied mostly in the southeast.
But Turkish officials have welcomed a recent crackdown on alleged PKK sympathisers by police in Britain and Belgium.
Amnesty International hopes to put to the test Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's promises to improve rights and solve the Kurdish issue through "Moslem brotherhood".
The head of the London-based rights group is due in Turkey on Thursday to try to hold talks with Erbakan although the government has not yet said it will agree to a meeting.
"If they don't hold the meeting it will tell a lot about the new government's human rights policy," Amnesty spokeswoman Anita Thiessen said.
Erbakan became Turkey's first ever Islamist leader in June. His coalition has taken few steps to end the Kurdish fighting by peaceful means.
Amnesty chief Pierre Sane will also try to see Islamist Justice Minister Sevket Kazan and right-wing Interior Minister Mehmet Agar.
